---
title: "Part 2 · The CRP bridge"
description: "One concentration parameter, read in the language of the Chinese restaurant process and stick-breaking: two lenses, the unintended prior, dominance, collapse, and what the vague default says."
---

Part 1 built the Dirichlet process mixture from stick-breaking and the Chinese restaurant
process. This part keeps that language and asks what a Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on the
concentration parameter alpha says about clusters. Eight widgets, in the order of the
argument:

**1. alpha is a pseudo-count for new tables.** In the
[Chinese restaurant process](../dpm/crp.qmd) customer n + 1 opens a new table with
probability alpha / (alpha + n). Everything below follows from that one rule.

**2. One alpha, two lenses.** The same alpha fixes how many clusters the J units occupy
(the count view, K_J) and how large a random unit's cluster is (the weight view, W_SB).
Only the first depends on J. A Gamma prior on alpha mixes many conditional pmfs into one.

| Page | Catalog | What it shows | Standalone |
|---|---|---|---|
| [One alpha, two lenses](two-lenses.qmd) | C-04 | K_J pmf, alpha density and W_SB density side by side; move J and only the count view moves | [embed](../../embed/two-lenses.html) |
| [Gamma mixing](gamma-mixing.qmd) | C-12 | Conditional pmfs at alpha nodes add up to the marginal pmf of K_J; 20 nodes versus 400 | [embed](../../embed/gamma-mixing.html) |

**3. The unintended prior, restaurant by restaurant.** Gamma(1.60, 1.22) at J = 50 gives
"about five clusters" and, in most restaurants, one table with more than half of the
customers.

| Page | Catalog | What it shows | Standalone |
|---|---|---|---|
| [The unintended prior in 1000 restaurants](crp-unintended.qmd) | M-05 | Table counts against the exact pmf, the largest table's share, and W_SB versus W_max | [embed](../../embed/crp-unintended.html) |

**4. Dominance and collapse.** The first stick-breaking piece is the size-biased weight
W_SB. How often it passes one half is majority-mass dominance; the largest piece W_max can
only be larger. Prior mass near alpha = 0 seats everyone at one table: collapse.

| Page | Catalog | What it shows | Standalone |

| [Dominance in stick-breaking rows](dominance.qmd#m-18-the-first-piece-is-not-always-the-largest) | M-18 | The same sticks in breaking order and by size: the first piece is not always the largest | [embed](../../embed/sb-vs-ranked.html) |
| [Dominance in stick-breaking rows](dominance.qmd#c-16-how-far-apart-can-w_sb-and-w_max-be) | C-16 | S(t) ≤ Pr(W_max > t) ≤ S(t)/t with the exact value, and STAR posterior summaries | [embed](../../embed/wmax-bounds.html) |

**5. What the default says.** Gamma(1, 1) is vague about alpha and definite about clusters.

| Page | Catalog | What it shows | Standalone |

::: {.callout-tip}
## In 60 seconds

Open [One alpha, two lenses](two-lenses.qmd), keep Gamma(1, 1), and drag J from 10 to 500:
the count view moves, the weight view does not. Then open
[Dominance](dominance.qmd), choose Gamma(1, 3) and press Redraw a few times: about four
rows in five have a first piece above one half (S(.5) = .812).
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Terms.** *Size-biased weight*, *dominance* (majority-mass: Pr(W_SB > .5); extreme:
Pr(W_SB > .9)) and *collapse* (prior P(K_J = 1) versus posterior Pr(K_J = 1 | data)) are
terms of the DPprior paper, not of Broderick's tutorials. K_J is the number of fitted
components (occupied clusters) among the J units. See the [vocabulary](../vocabulary.qmd).
The restaurant and stick-breaking pictures follow Broderick (MLSS 2016; 2012 tutorial);
the mathematics is re-implemented and no code is copied.
:::
